title: Cloud Adoption and Migration
overview: Choose a migration approach by diagnosing the application’s business and technical problems. Compare VMs, containers, IaaS and PaaS, then apply the migration options and six modernisation drivers. Assess dependencies, risk and total cost, including the temporary cost bubble, before sequencing an incremental migration.
big_ideas: VMs include a guest OS; containers share a kernel and typically start faster with lower overhead. Image size and startup time vary.
Choose among Rehost, Replatform, Rearchitect, Rebuild and Replace; Retain, Retire and Encapsulate are alternatives. Their IaaS/PaaS/SaaS mapping is illustrative, not mandatory.
Lift-and-shift favours speed and low initial effort; lift-and-optimise can improve ongoing cost and return at greater migration effort.
Pick the approach per application by diagnosing it with the six drivers: business fit, innovation, agility (business) and cost, complexity, risk (IT).
The more you change (infrastructure, then platform, then code, then functionality), the higher the potential value, but also the cost, time and risk.
Expect a temporary migration bubble of extra cost (duplicate environments, training, consulting, lease penalties) before savings appear.
Start with a low-risk workload you can learn from, not the highest-ROI one; then rinse and repeat.
Decide sourcing (internal vs partner) and hosting (data centre/IaaS/PaaS/SaaS) with weighted criteria: differentiation, operational complexity, skills.

sections.title: Recap: VMs, containers, managed services and IaaS
sections.summary: How VMs and containers package applications, what managed cloud services are, why IaaS emerged and which workloads suit it.

items: **VM** → boots a **guest OS** via a **hypervisor**
**Container** → starts **isolated processes** sharing the **host kernel**
**Containers** → usually **less overhead**, **faster startup**; **image pulls** and **application initialisation** still take time
**VMs suit** → **different OS requirements** or **stronger kernel separation**

items.t: **Grew out of successive waves of sharing**:

sub: freeing the business to **focus on core work**

items.t: Hand **part or all of cloud operations** to a provider:

items: Usually on **subscription**
**Contracted before migrating**
Client gets **cloud benefit** with **less internal time and cost**
**IaC** → infrastructure as **machine-readable definition files**, not **manual setup** → makes IaaS **repeatable**

items.t: An IaaS platform is run by **three back-end systems**:

terms.def: Partial or full management of a client's cloud resources by a provider, usually on subscription.
Provisioning infrastructure from machine-readable definition files rather than manual setup.
Virtual Infrastructure Manager: the component that manages VMs and images in an IaaS cloud.

check.q: A team moved from VMs to containers to cut scale-out time, but new replicas still take 90 seconds to serve traffic. What is the likely cause, and what would you check?

items: **Containers skip booting a guest OS** because they **share the host kernel**
**Likely cause**: **pulling a large image**, **loading dependencies** and **initialising the application** can still **dominate startup**
**Check**: **image size** and **pull time**, and how long the application takes to **warm up**
a.foot: **Smaller images** and **lighter initialisation** help more than changing the **isolation boundary**.

check.q: A legacy app needs a Windows kernel feature, and a second workload from a different tenant must run on the same hosts with strong separation. VMs or containers for each?

items: **Legacy app** needs **its own OS** → a container **sharing the host kernel** cannot provide it
**Hypervisor boundary** → **stronger separation between tenants** than **process-level isolation**
a.foot: You give up the **lighter weight** and **faster startup** of containers, which matter less for these two requirements.

check.q: A company with a 3-person IT team wants to migrate to the cloud this year but has no cloud skills. Should it run the migration itself or use a managed cloud service, and what is the catch?

items: A provider takes on **migration, configuration, optimisation, security and maintenance**, usually on **subscription**
→ the **small team** gets cloud benefits without **building every skill first**
**Catch**: the **ongoing subscription cost** and **dependence on the provider**
The **contract** must be in place **before migrating**
a.foot: The company still **owns its data and decisions**.

sections.title: OpenStack and Ansible (IaaS as code)
sections.summary: OpenStack as an open-source IaaS platform and Ansible as a way to provision it as code.

notes.lead: Open-source suite that turns hardware into a private IaaS cloud.
items: **Compute** → **Nova**
**Networking** → **Neutron**
**Object and block storage** → **Swift**, **Cinder**
**Identity** → **Keystone**
**VM templates** → **Glance**
**Dashboard** → **Horizon**
**Orchestration** → **Heat**
**Provisions and configures** systems using **ordered YAML playbooks**
**Modules** can express **intended resource state** without a **resident target agent**
**Heat** uses its own YAML format, **HOT**, for OpenStack orchestration
A **Heat template is not an Ansible playbook**
Whole environment is **versioned and re-runnable** instead of **hand-built**
**OpenStack-Ansible** → a common way to **install OpenStack itself**

terms.def: Open-source software suite for building a private IaaS cloud (Nova, Neutron, Swift, Cinder, Keystone, etc.).
A YAML file listing tasks Ansible runs to provision or configure systems.
Heat Orchestration Template: OpenStack's YAML template format for orchestration.

check.q: A university wants a private IaaS cloud on its own hardware and asks what a hypervisor alone would be missing. Using OpenStack's components, explain.

a.lead: A **hypervisor runs VMs**, but an **IaaS cloud** needs more.

items.t: **OpenStack** supplies these on top of **compute (Nova)**, for example:

items: **Without them** → users still depend on **administrators** to wire each VM together → fails **on-demand self-service**

check.q: A security team won't allow extra agents on production servers but wants the servers' configuration managed as code. Does Ansible fit, and what does it still need?

items: **No resident agent** has to be installed on each target

sub: whatever **prerequisites its modules require** on the target

a.foot: The security team's concern then shifts to protecting those **credentials** and the **control node**.

check.q: An engineer calls an Ansible playbook a Heat template 'because both are YAML' and wants to feed the playbook to Heat. What is wrong?

items: **Ansible** runs a **playbook's ordered tasks**
**Heat** interprets **HOT templates** to **orchestrate OpenStack resources**
Each tool needs **its own format**
a.foot: Either can describe **infrastructure as code**: choose by whether you need **OpenStack-native orchestration** or **general provisioning and configuration** across systems.

center.label: OpenStack
center.detail: Open-source suite that turns hardware into a private IaaS cloud; Ansible can provision and install it.

sections.title: PaaS and containers vs VMs
sections.summary: Why PaaS emerged, what it gives, which workloads fit it, the CNCF ecosystem, and the VM vs container comparison.

items: Platform supplies **deployment**, **scaling** and **runtime management** for developers
Lecture's large **labour, capital and delivery-time reductions** → **illustrative benefits**, not **guaranteed savings** for every workload
Teams still **configure access** and **secure their code**

notes.h: Compute abstraction moves up the stack
items: **Mainframe**
**Client-server**
**Web**
Now **containers** with **edge devices**
notes.foot: The **CNCF** (**Linux Foundation**) hosts the **open-source projects** behind cloud-native computing.

items: **Virtualization** → **hardware-level** vs **OS-level**
**Isolation** → **machines** vs **processes**
**Resources** → via **hypervisor** vs **kernel namespaces and cgroups**
**Strength** → **hardware flexibility** vs **portability**
**VMs** bring **established management/security tools**; **containers** bring **lightness and speed**

terms.def: Cloud Native Computing Foundation: Linux Foundation body hosting cloud-native projects such as Kubernetes.
Linux kernel features that give containers isolated views of the system (namespaces) and resource limits (cgroups).
Software (Type 1 or Type 2) that runs multiple VMs on one physical machine.

check.q: A team's API uses a managed database, a queue and CI/CD, and needs no OS changes. A second system is a backup server that needs custom storage drivers. Which fits PaaS and which IaaS?

items: **API → PaaS**: consumes **managed platform services**; the platform takes over **deployment, scaling and runtime management**
**Backup server → IaaS**: needs **server-level control** of **drivers and storage**
a.foot: With PaaS the team still **configures access** and **secures its own code**.

check.q: A vendor pitch says moving to PaaS will 'cut delivery time from months to hours'. How would you treat this claim in a business case?

a.lead: As an **illustrative benefit**, not a **guaranteed saving**.
items: **PaaS removes server setup** and **platform operations** → can shorten delivery a great deal
**Real gain** depends on how much of the current delay is **infrastructure work** rather than **design, testing or approvals**
**Measure** the **current lead time** and its **causes** before promising a figure

check.q: A multi-tenant SaaS platform plans to run every customer's code in containers on shared hosts. A security reviewer objects. What is the concern, and what are the options?

items: **Concern**: containers isolate processes through **kernel namespaces and cgroups** but **share the host kernel** → a **kernel exploit** can reach **other tenants**
**VMs** isolate at the **hardware level** through a **hypervisor** and come with **established security tooling**

sub: **containers grouped onto VMs by tenant** → keeps most of the containers' **speed**

sections.title: Migration framework and strategy
sections.summary: How to think about migration: an on-prem to AWS example, the AWS migration roadmap, lift-and-shift vs lift-and-optimize, and Gartner's six drivers of modernization.

notes.lead: Migration is a decision process, not a single move.
items: **Discover and assess**
**Plan and sequence**
**Migrate and UAT**
**Tune**
**Sign off**
**Cut over** and **operate**
notes.foot: Alongside throughout: **org/ops impact analysis** and **change management**.

notes.lead: Trades initial speed against later optimisation.
items: **Lift-and-shift** → moves **largely unchanged** apps **quickly**; may **preserve inefficient resource use**
**Lift-and-optimise** → **adapts during migration**; usually **longer** and **costs more initially**, for potential **ongoing cost and ROI improvements**
**TCO** → a **cost to minimise**
**ROI** → a **return to improve**

sub: **Risk** → security, compliance, supportability, scalability, skills shortage

items: **Understand** each approach's **scope and effect**
Run a **cause-effect analysis** with the six drivers → find the **functional, architectural and technological problems**
**Pick an approach per application** with **Gartner's framework**
**DNS**
**Load balancing**
**Auto-scaling web/app fleets** across **two AZs**
**Managed database**

terms.def: Move an application to the cloud with minimal or no change.
Migrate and adapt the application to use cloud services at the same time.
An isolated data-centre location within a cloud region; spreading across AZs gives resilience.

check.q: A firm must leave its data centre in 4 months and its apps are over-provisioned. Lift-and-shift or lift-and-optimise?

items: The **deadline** and **low initial change** matter most
It **carries the over-provisioning** into the cloud → budget for **right-sizing and optimisation after cutover**
**Lift-and-optimise** → lower **ongoing TCO** and **improves ROI sooner**, but **takes longer** and **costs more up front**
a.foot: The **4-month window** doesn't allow lift-and-optimise.

check.q: A business owner says 'our app is too expensive, let's rewrite it as microservices'. Using the six drivers, what would you check before agreeing?

items: **Driver is cost** (infrastructure too expensive for the value) → **Rehost** or **Replatform** may fix it far more cheaply
**Rewrite justified** when the drivers are **business fit, innovation or agility** → the app can't **meet needs** or **change fast enough**
**Cause-effect analysis** → shows whether the problem is **functional, architectural or technological**
The option should **fix that cause**

check.q: The migration roadmap lists 'do not move' and 'decommission' as paths alongside lift-and-shift and refactor. Why is it worth assessing every application before picking a default path?

items: Some apps are better **left in place** or **switched off** → moving them **wastes effort** and adds **cloud cost**
**Discover and assess** each app first, then **plan and sequence by dependency**
→ avoids **migrating something only to retire it later**
a.foot: Cost: the time spent on **discovery** before anything moves.

items.label: Business fit
items.detail: The application no longer meets business requirements; investigate whether its functions must change.

items.label: Innovation
items.detail: The application blocks a new opportunity; identify the missing business capability.

items.label: Agility
items.detail: Changes cannot keep pace with the business; investigate architecture and coupling.

items.label: Cost
items.detail: Operating and changing the application costs too much relative to its business value.

items.label: Complexity
items.detail: Structure or technology makes maintenance and change risky or expensive.

items.label: Risk
items.detail: IT driver: security, compliance, supportability, scalability, skills shortage.

sections.title: Migration options I: Rehost and Replatform
sections.summary: The option spectrum against IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, and the two lightest-touch options with typical use cases.

items: **Retire**
**Rehost**
**Replatform**
**Rearchitect**
**Rebuild**
**Replace**
notes.foot: Roughly: **IaaS** ≈ Rehost; **PaaS** ≈ Replatform through Rebuild; **SaaS** ≈ Replace.

items: Moves the app to **other infrastructure**
**No recompiling**; **no change to code, features or functions**
Moves to a **new runtime platform** with **minimal compatibility changes**
Examples: **managed cloud database**, **serverless**, **auto-scaling**
**No change to code structure or features**
**Rehost** → changes **only where it runs**
**Replatform** → also **swaps platform pieces** (database, runtime); app stays **functionally the same**

terms.def: Redeploy unchanged to new infrastructure (lift and shift).
Move to a new runtime platform with minimal code changes (lift, shape and shift).

check.q: A bank wants its transaction system on a managed cloud database but cannot touch the business logic. Rehost or Replatform?

items: **Swaps the platform** (the database) with **minimal compatibility changes**; **code structure and features** stay the same
**Rehost** would move the app with its existing **self-managed database unchanged**
a.foot: Replatform adds **testing for database compatibility** in exchange for **less database operations work**.

check.q: After a Rehost, the business asks why the app's features and slow reports didn't improve. Is the migration a failure?

items: **Rehost changes only where the app runs** → its benefits are **infrastructure** ones
**Faster reports or new features** → need **Replatform** (e.g. a **managed analytics service**) or deeper options
a.foot: Set those **expectations in the business case**.

check.q: A retailer's app runs fine but the database can't cope with holiday peaks, and the code must not change. What option fits, and what would push you further along the spectrum?

items: Addresses the **peaks** without touching **code structure**
**What pushes further**: the **code itself blocks scaling** (e.g. **shared state in the app tier**) → Replatform won't be enough → **Rearchitect**
a.foot: Rearchitect comes at **higher cost and risk**.

visuals.title: Migration options are alternatives
rows: Runtime or platform; minimal code edits
visuals.caption: These are choices per workload, not a required sequence. Encapsulate exposes retained functionality through APIs.

sections.title: Migration options II: Rearchitect to Encapsulate
sections.summary: The deeper-change options (Rearchitect, Rebuild) and the non-migrating or replacing options (Replace, Retain, Retire, Encapsulate).

items: **Restructures code** without **changing external behaviour**
Goal → remove **technical debt**, improve **non-functional qualities**
→ components **scale independently**
**Writes the application afresh**, even as a **like-for-like replacement**
Usually **cloud-native**
**Rearchitect** → **keeps behaviour**, **reshapes the existing code**
**Rebuild** → may **change functionality too**; **highest value, cost and risk**
**Replace (repurchase, drop and shop)** → swaps the app for a **COTS or SaaS product**, taking **new requirements** into account
**Retire** → **decommissions** it, often **as part of a Replace**
**Retain** → leave the app **as is for now**

sub: modernization **not worth the effort and risk**

items: **Encapsulate** → exposes the app's **data and functions as API services**
Encapsulate **extends its value** while **hiding the implementation**

terms.def: Restructure code/architecture without changing external behaviour, e.g. to microservices or serverless.
Rewrite the application from scratch, often cloud-native.
Drop the app and buy COTS/SaaS instead.
Wrap an existing app behind APIs so its functions can be reused as services.
Commercial off-the-shelf software.

check.q: An app's features are fine, but one module can't scale and every change is risky because of technical debt. A teammate proposes Rebuild. Do you agree?

a.lead: **Rearchitect** is the better fit, not Rebuild.
items: **Rearchitect**: restructures the existing code **without changing external behaviour** → e.g. **extract the bottleneck module** so it **scales independently**
It reduces **technical debt**
**Rebuild**: **rewrites everything**, carries the **highest cost and risk**
a.foot: Rebuild is justified only when **new capabilities** such as **mobile-first, IoT or AI** are needed.

check.q: A mainframe holds valuable pricing logic that a new mobile app needs, but the mainframe is too risky to change this year. Retain, Encapsulate or Rebuild?

items: Expose the **pricing data and functions as APIs** → the mobile app uses them **without rewriting the internals**
**Plain Retain** → leaves the logic **inaccessible** to the new app
**Rebuild** → the **risk** the business wants to avoid
a.foot: Cost: the **legacy system stays in place**, and its **performance and availability** now **limit the new app**.

check.q: A department's expense tool is home-grown, offers nothing unique, and its developer has left. Which option fits, and what goes with it?

a.lead: **Replace** with a **COTS or SaaS** product, and **Retire** the old tool as part of the move.
items: Take **current requirements** into account
**Not a differentiator** → **owning code adds no value**
a.foot: Cost: **users adapt** to the product's **workflow**, and **data has to be migrated** before **decommissioning**.

sections.title: Choosing the approach and planning
sections.summary: Gartner's comparison of what each option changes and its trade-offs, Gartner's migration stages, and the seven-step plan with eight classification criteria.

notes.h: More change: more value, cost, risk
items: **Rehost** → changes **only infrastructure**
**Replatform** → adds **platform/data layers**
**Rearchitect** → adds **configuration and custom code**
**Rebuild** and **Replace** → can change **everything**, including **business logic and UX**
**Rehost** → **lowest overall**
**Rebuild** → **highest** on **change, value, cost and risk**
**Replace** → most **business disruption**
notes.foot: Pick the **lightest option** that **fixes the diagnosed drivers**.

notes.h: Gartner's four steps: mass migration to IaaS
items: **Choose the approach** → **lift-and-shift vs lift-and-optimize**, weighing **lock-in** against **unique cloud value**
**Build the business case**
**Migrate and optimize** → use **cloud-native services sooner**
**Identify desired outcomes**
**Classify cloud candidates**
**Define service and deployment criteria** per workload (**IaaS/PaaS/SaaS** and **public/private** placement)
**Devise an iterative agile process** → **fails fast and learns fast**
**Get buy-in**
**Start simple** → **prioritize learning over ROI**
**Rinse and repeat**
**Architecture**
**Security**
**Availability**
**Performance**
**Scalability**
**Strategic importance**
**Future plans**
**Enthusiasm of the team**
notes.foot: First project → **low-risk and highly instructive**, not the **highest-ROI** one: **early success builds skills and buy-in**.

terms.def: A pre-configured, secure cloud environment and architecture set up before workloads are migrated.
Dependence on one provider's unique services that makes switching costly.
Agile migration mindset: small iterations that surface problems early.

check.q: Rebuild scores highest on value in Gartner's comparison. Why is it not the default answer?

items: Rebuild also has the **highest cost of change**, the **highest risk** and a **long time to value**
**Diagnosed drivers only call for infrastructure or platform fixes** → **Rehost** or **Replatform** give **faster, cheaper, lower-risk** results
**Choose the lightest option** that **fixes the drivers**
a.foot: Keep **Rebuild** for when **business logic or UX must change**.

check.q: Leadership wants the first cloud migration to be the system with the biggest projected ROI, a customer-facing billing platform. How do you respond?

items: **Seven-step plan**: **start simple** and **prioritise learning over ROI**
**First project** should be **low-risk** and **highly instructive** → **early success** builds **skills and buy-in**
**Billing platform** is **strategically important** and **high-risk** → a failure would **set back the whole programme**
a.foot: Migrate it in a **later wave**, once the **landing zone** and **operating model** have been proven.

check.q: Two candidate first workloads score the same on architecture, security, availability and performance. One team is eager, the other was told to migrate. Which would you pick?

items: **Team enthusiasm** is one of the **eight classification criteria** → migrations need the **owning team's engagement**
**A willing team** → an **early success** and **useful lessons** more likely
The other workload can follow once there is a **proven pattern to copy**

steps.label: Desired outcomes
steps.detail: Identify what you want from cloud.

steps.label: Classify candidates
steps.detail: Eight criteria: architecture, security, availability, performance, scalability, strategic importance, future plans, team enthusiasm.

steps.label: Deployment criteria
steps.detail: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS or private per workload.

steps.label: Get buy-in
steps.detail: Show the top-down or bottom-up support needed across the organization.

steps.label: Start simple
steps.detail: Low-risk, highly instructive first project; prioritise learning over ROI.

sections.title: Application concerns and assessment
sections.summary: What to assess in each application, the migration planning framework, the migration cost bubble and TCO.

notes.h: Assess each app across concern families
items: **Performance** → elasticity, latency, throughput
**Architecture** → complexity, data, life expectancy
**Financial** → operating cost, business value
**Risk** → business criticality, technical, contractual, audit
**Operations** → continuity, tooling, deployment
**Security/compliance** → jurisdiction, regulation, privacy, encryption; can **rule out regions or providers**

sub: **portfolio analysis** assigning **an R to each app**

items: **Design the target**
Follow a **road map** to **migration complete**
notes.foot: Supported by **stakeholder buy-in**, **quality assurance**, **risk mitigation** and a **scope/schedule plan**.

items: **Discovery**
**Duplicate environments**
**Training**
**Consultants**
**Tools**
**Lease penalties**
notes.foot: Compare **lifetime TCO** with the **baseline**; **retirement and optimisation** may produce savings, but only the **business case** can establish **whether and when** they occur.

terms.def: Temporary cost increase from migration activities and overlapping environments; later savings depend on the business case.
Total Cost of Ownership: full lifetime cost of running a system, used to compare on-prem vs cloud.
Reviewing all applications to assign each a migration decision (the R options).

check.q: Six months into migration, a CFO sees costs higher than before and wants to stop. What is the likely explanation, and what would you show?

items: **Costs rise temporarily**: **duplicate environments, training, consultants, tools and lease penalties**
→ until **old infrastructure is retired** and **optimisation** starts
**Show**: **lifetime TCO** against the **baseline**, and the **dates when on-premises costs stop**
a.foot: The CFO's concern is valid if the **business case never showed savings**, or **retirement keeps slipping**.

check.q: An app processes citizens' health records and must stay within national borders. The preferred provider has no local region. How does this assessment concern affect the plan?

a.lead: **Jurisdiction and regulation** can **rule out regions or providers** → that provider is **excluded** for this app, no matter what else it offers.

sub: a **private or hybrid placement** for the records

items: **Encryption and privacy controls** are still needed, but they **don't remove** a **data-location rule**

check.q: A portfolio analysis assigns Rehost to an app with 2 years of remaining life and high audit risk. Which assessment concerns would make you question that choice?

items: **2 years left** → **Retain** or **Retire** may cost less than migrating
**Audit risk** → check **compliance in the target environment** before moving
The **planning framework** expects each app's **R** to come from these **concerns**, not from a **default**

sections.title: Sourcing and hosting models
sections.summary: Deciding who should run each capability and where it should be hosted, using weighted criteria, then the overall assessment approach.

items: **Sourcing model** → **who operates it**: **internal team** or a **partner** (e.g. **MSP** or **cloud product partner**)
**Hosting model** → **where it runs**: **own data centre**, **IaaS**, **PaaS** or **SaaS**
**Level of differentiation** → **core stays internal**; **non-differentiators go to partners**
**Complexity of business processes** → **complex stays internal**
**Skills** → **common skills in-house**; **highly specialized skills outsourced**
notes.foot: **Core, complex, commonly skilled** → lean **internal**; **non-differentiating, simple, specialized** → lean **partner**.

items: **Rate each criterion 1-3** and **weight** it
**Skills scored inversely** → **1 means highly specialized**
Combine into a **composite classification**
**Validate with stakeholders**
**Compare pros and cons** of alternatives
Use a **proof of concept** to **reduce risk**

terms.def: Who operates a capability: internal team or partner (MSP / product partner).
Where it runs: data centre, IaaS, PaaS or SaaS.
Managed Service Provider that runs operations for you.

check.q: A company's CRM is not a differentiator, has simple processes, and needs specialist skills it cannot hire. What sourcing and hosting model would you suggest?

a.lead: **Partner** sourcing, most likely **SaaS** hosting → effectively a **Replace** decision.
items: **All three sourcing factors** point to a **partner**
**Gives up**: **deep customisation** and **control of the roadmap**
a.foot: Acceptable for a **non-differentiating** capability.

check.q: A trading firm's pricing engine is its main differentiator and has complex logic, but it needs rare low-latency skills. The sourcing factors conflict. How do you decide?

items: **Differentiation carries the most weight** (**60%** in the example) → outweighs **skills** pointing to a **partner**
**Skills gap** → **hiring or training**, or use a **partner** only for **specialised infrastructure work**
a.foot: **Validate with stakeholders**: the weights are a **decision aid**, not a rule.

check.q: Using the example weights, a capability scores differentiation 3, complexity 2 and skills 1. What does the result suggest, and what should you do with it?

items: **Result** → leans toward **internal sourcing** in the example
**Skills is scored inversely** → the **1** means **highly specialised skills** are needed → a real **gap to plan for**
**Validate** against **actual skills and constraints**, and test risky choices with a **proof of concept**

exam_angles.q: A hospital's 15-year-old on-premises patient scheduling system slows down at morning peaks. The code is stable and meets business needs, but the database server is end-of-life, and patient data must stay in the country. Recommend a migration option, justify it with the drivers, and name two risks to manage.

a.lead: **Replatform**: move to a **managed database** and **auto-scaling** in an **in-country region**, with **minimal code change**.
items: **Drivers**: **risk** (**end-of-life platform**) and **scalability**, not **business fit**
**Not Rebuild** → would add **cost and risk** without fixing anything the business needs

sub: **database compatibility** → test on the new engine, ideally with a **proof of concept**

a.foot: Budget for the **migration bubble** while **both environments run**.

exam_angles.q: A firm must exit its data centre in 6 months, with 80 apps, many over-provisioned. The CFO expects savings in year one. Compare lift-and-shift and lift-and-optimise, recommend a mix, and respond to the CFO.

sub: needs the **least initial change** and **fits the deadline**
but **takes longer** and **costs more up front**
**lift-and-shift for most apps**, **sequenced by dependency and risk**
**optimisation** only for a **few high-cost apps** that can be done in time

items.t: **To the CFO**: year one includes the **migration bubble**

exam_angles.q: Design a portfolio assessment for an organisation with 200 applications and a 2-year programme. How would you decide each app's R, and which app would you migrate first?

sub: the **application concerns**: **performance, architecture, financial, risk, operations, security and compliance**

items: **Diagnose** each app's problem with the **six drivers**
**Assign the lightest R** that fixes it, using the **sourcing and hosting scoring** to decide **who runs it and where**
**Choose the first migration** on the **eight criteria**: **low-risk**, **instructive**, with an **enthusiastic team**, **not the highest ROI**
**Iterate in waves** and compare **TCO against the baseline**

exam_angles.q: An insurer's 30-year-old policy system holds valuable rules, is nearly impossible to change, and is due to be replaced by a SaaS product in 3 years. A new mobile app needs policy data now. Choose between Retain, Encapsulate and Rebuild, and say what changes if the SaaS project is cancelled.

a.lead: **Encapsulate**: expose **policy data and functions through APIs**, hiding the internals.
items: The mobile app can use them **now**; the system **stays in place** until the **planned Replace**
**Not Rebuild** → would **duplicate work** the **SaaS replacement** will make redundant
**Not plain Retain** → would leave the mobile app **without data**
**Risk**: the legacy system's **availability and performance** now **limit the mobile app**

items.t: **If the SaaS project is cancelled**: **revisit the drivers**
sub: a **Rearchitect or Rebuild behind the same APIs** becomes the **long-term path**
the **APIs** let you **swap the implementation** without **breaking the app**

exam_angles.q: A team migrating a 3-tier app proposes containers instead of VMs for the web and app tiers, keeping the database on a VM. Evaluate the proposal, including where containers would be the wrong choice.

items: **Containers**: **lighter**, usually **start faster**, **package the app consistently**, and let **each tier scale on its own**
**Database**: keep it on a **VM** or move it to a **managed database** if it needs **OS-level tuning** or **strong isolation**
**Wrong choice** where a workload needs a **different OS kernel** or **strong tenant separation** → containers **share the host kernel**
a.foot: Actual **startup gains** depend on **image size** and **application initialisation**.
